title: Crowdfunding for Emergencies: an UN-OCHA Think Brief
html:
In October 2013, I wrote a post - Kickstarting an Emergency - discussing the need for a humanitarian crowdfunding solution and outlined why I believed that one was needed.  A month later, I was in the Philippines responding to Typhoon Haiyan where my beliefs were solidified.  What did I see that cemented these beliefs? A member of the affected community had sent a few photos to an unaffected family member in Cebu city. The recipient put these photos onto a simple website, attached a PayPal button and started promoting the site through his personal networks. It took less than an hour and anyone in the world could deposit money directly to the affected person’s Paypal account. Money was moving into the affected areas when it was needed. At the same time I knew that there were many practicalities that made this approach unscalable and could eventually scare those wanting to donate (think risk of potential abuse).

In the summer of 2014, I paired up with Javier Salazar and Roxanne Moore to better understand the various models, frameworks, platforms and risks related to crowdfunding and how they should be applied to the humanitarian sector. It took some work, including needing to understand what happened in emergencies that occurred before we finished drafting (e.g. Ebola and the Nepal earthquake), but I am excited to have our paper now released.  In August, UN-OCHA released it as a Think Brief: Crowdfunding for Emergencies.

Download PDF

Things are only becoming easier for people who want to crowdfund. As IRIN outlined in their article about crowdfunding, “Setting up an appeal requires only a bank account, an internet connection and a few minutes.” More of the commercial platforms are dedicating capacity and space to disaster response. Websites are easier than ever to create. Moving money is easy and fast.  But, how do we provide a trustworthy solution that can scale to be used in any emergency (sudden onset or protracted), improve transparency and accountability, ensure funding does not “harm”, move money to the affected in hours, and minimize any potential risk of abuse?

In our paper, we explored these topics and more. We discuss and evaluate different crowdfunding models (donation-based, reward-based, debt-based, and equity-based) eventually suggesting a hybrid model combining donation and reward-based models. Determining the appropriate platform model for an emergency context is important, but developing a strong implementation and financial distribution framework is also critical. The paper examines the concepts of single-goal, multi-stage goals, and distributed-goals as different possible options that could be supported. We studied the different commercial crowdfunding platforms and how close they came to meeting our ideal needs.

We also addressed the biggest challenge of all - trust. We discussed: How do you know the money will be used as intended?; How do you know the money does not cause a problem (good for one, but not for the larger community)?; How do you ensure that the result is sustainable?; and How do you ensure accountability of the project initiator?. Do you build these aspects into the technical system? Or, do you have independant services verify the project initiators before they can post a funding request? Or, does it require a strong combination of the two?

So, what did we recommend? In short, we settled on the ideal option being be a gamified, certified donation-based/reward-based hybrid crowdfunding model using a distributed-goal framework with get-what-you-reach fundraising goals and low moderating owner charges (approximately 5 per cent). Yes, it is quite a mouthful. But, when the right organizations are ready to make it work, I suspect we could see a major shift in how emergencies are funded.

Andrej
